p.src: Classical mechanics is not only a collection of equations for falling bodies, orbiting planets, or charged particles. Before choosing any particular equation, we can ask a more general question: what must a law of motion look like in order to count as a classical law? We shall begin with systems so simple that every possible history can be drawn on the blackboard. Once the ideas of state, determinism, reversibility, and conservation are clear there, we shall return to particles moving in ordinary space.

p.src: Two Kinds of Question

u.src: Two Kinds of Question
en: Two Kinds of Question

p.src: There are two kinds of question in mechanics. One asks for the specific law that governs a particular system. A planet moving in the gravitational field of a massive body obeys one law; an electrically charged particle moving in a magnetic field obeys another. These are questions about the detailed laws of nature.

p.src: The other question concerns the framework common to all such examples. Are there rules that every allowable law must satisfy? Which features belong to classical mechanics itself, independently of the force or the object under study? The specific examples will illustrate the answer, but it is this second question that organizes the subject.

p.src: The most useful first example is an abstract coin on an abstract table. We retain only one property of the coin: it can show heads or tails. Its space of configurations is therefore $\mathcal C=\{H,T\}.$ The word configuration means one of the possible ways the system can be. An initial condition is a choice of one of them. A one-sided coin would be still simpler, but it would have only one configuration and nothing could ever happen. Two states are enough to make dynamics possible.

p.src: The Coin: State, Law, and History

u.src: The Coin: State, Law, and History
en: The Coin: State, Law, and History

p.src:
Let time advance in integer steps, as if the world were illuminated by a stroboscope: $t=\ldots,-2,-1,0,1,2,\ldots .$ A law of motion is an update rule. It assigns to the state at time $t$ a state at time $t+1$. The simplest rule does nothing: $H\longmapsto H,
  \qquad
  T\longmapsto T.$ Starting from $H$, the entire history is $H,H,H,\ldots$; starting from $T$, it is $T,T,T,\ldots$. The rule is boring, but it is completely predictive.

p.src:
The other reversible rule exchanges the two states: $H\longmapsto T,
  \qquad
  T\longmapsto H.$ The histories now alternate: $H,T,H,T,\ldots,
  \qquad
  T,H,T,H,\ldots .$ An arrow points from the state before the update to the state after it. Thus the tail of an arrow says where the system starts and the arrowhead says where it goes.

p.src:
We can encode the faces by a two-valued variable, $\sigma=
  \begin{cases}
    +1,&H,\\
    -1,&T.
  \end{cases}$ The letter $\sigma$ is traditionally used for two-valued quantities in physics, especially in descriptions of spin, although no knowledge of spin is needed here. In this notation the two rules become equations of motion: $\begin{aligned}
  \sigma(t+1)&=\sigma(t),
  &&\text{identity law},\\
  \sigma(t+1)&=-\sigma(t),
  &&\text{flip law}.\end{aligned}$ The variable does not add new physics. It gives a compact label for the configuration and turns a graph into an equation.

p.src: For either rule, the initial state and the law determine the state at every later time. This statement presumes that the system is closed. If someone reaches in and turns the coin, then the hand is an external influence not included in our description. We have not disproved determinism; we have changed the system. A classical law is intended to govern a closed system, with all influences relevant to its evolution included.

p.src:
A genuinely different law divides the six states into two cycles, for example $1\to2\to3\to1,
  \qquad
  4\to6\to5\to4.$ There is still one die and one law, but a trajectory that begins on one cycle can never reach the other. We may attach a number $Q$ to the cycles, $Q=
  \begin{cases}
    0,&\text{on the cycle }\{1,2,3\},\\
    1,&\text{on the cycle }\{4,5,6\}.
  \end{cases}$ The state changes at every step while $Q$ does not.

p.src: Infinite State Spaces

u.src: Infinite State Spaces
en: Infinite State Spaces

p.src: An infinite number of states does not require infinitely many objects. Take one particle constrained to the integer sites of an infinite line. Its state is an integer $n\in\mathbb Z.$ One law moves it one site to the right at every step: $n(t+1)=n(t)+1.$ This orbit never closes, but it passes through every integer if it is followed through both future and past. In that extended sense it plays the role of one endless cycle.

In that extended sense it plays the role of one endless cycle.

p.src:
Another law moves two sites at a time: $n(t+1)=n(t)+2.$ Now even sites evolve only through even sites, and odd sites only through odd sites. Parity is conserved: $\begin{aligned}
    Q_{\rm parity}(n)&=n\bmod 2,\\
    Q_{\rm parity}(n(t+1))&=Q_{\rm parity}(n(t)).
  \end{aligned}$ The passage from finite to infinite configuration space permits histories that never repeat, but it does not change the meanings of state, orbit, or conservation.

p.src: Determinism Is Not Yet Reversibility

u.src: Determinism Is Not Yet Reversibility
en: Determinism Is Not Yet Reversibility

p.src:
We now draw a rule that predicts the future uniquely but fails a second classical requirement. Give a three-sided coin the states heads, tails, and edge, and define $H\to T,
  \qquad
  T\to E,
  \qquad
  E\to T.$ Starting from $H$, the history is $H,T,E,T,E,\ldots;$ starting from either $T$ or $E$, the subsequent alternation is equally unambiguous. There is exactly one outgoing arrow at each state, so the rule is deterministic toward the future.

p.src: The difficulty appears when we try to reconstruct the past. If the present state is $T$, the preceding state could have been $H$ or $E$. Two histories have merged. Reverse every arrow and the defect becomes immediate: from $T$, the reversed graph offers two possible moves. The reverse rule is not deterministic.

p.src: A discrete law is reversible when the present state determines both a unique next state and a unique previous state. In a state graph, every state must have exactly one outgoing arrow and exactly one incoming arrow.

p.src: For a finite state space, a reversible update is a permutation of the states. It never creates or destroys distinctions among states; it only rearranges them. This is why its graph decomposes into cycles. The map in Eq.  is a function, but not a one-to-one function, and therefore has no inverse.

p.src: An exact law does not produce an exact forecast when the initial condition is known only approximately. p.src: Suppose the true initial state lies within a small region of possible states. Under some dynamics that region remains small for a long time; under others, nearby initial states separate rapidly. In a chaotic system, small initial uncertainties eventually grow into large differences. The atmosphere is a familiar example. Better measurements can extend the useful forecast, but for any fixed measurement accuracy there is a sufficiently distant time at which the forecast becomes unreliable.

p.src: A vector is an object with magnitude and direction. The displacement from the origin to a point is a vector, but vectors also describe velocity, acceleration, electric fields, and many other quantities. We shall write a vector in boldface, such as $\mathbf v$, and its magnitude as $\lvert\mathbf v\rvert$. The magnitude is nonnegative and vanishes only for the zero vector.

p.src: Geometrically, a vector is a free arrow. Translating the arrow without changing its length or direction does not change the vector. In a particular application a vector can be attached to a point, as when we specify the electric field at a given location, but attachment is extra information and not part of the abstract vector itself.

p.src:
Relative to Cartesian axes, a vector has components $\mathbf v=(v_x,v_y,v_z).$ The components are ordinary signed numbers, obtained by projection on the axes. They encode both magnitude and direction. The three-dimensional Pythagorean theorem gives $\lvert\mathbf v\rvert^2
  =v_x^2+v_y^2+v_z^2,
  \qquad
  \lvert\mathbf v\rvert
  =\sqrt{v_x^2+v_y^2+v_z^2}.$ The ratios of the components determine the direction. A negative component means that the vector points partly along the negative direction of that axis.

p.src: Multiplication by a real number changes a vector’s length and, if the number is negative, reverses its direction. For $c>0$, $c\mathbf A$ points in the direction of $\mathbf A$ and has magnitude $c\lvert\mathbf A\rvert$. In particular, $-\mathbf A$ has the same length as $\mathbf A$ and points oppositely.

p.src:
There are three equivalent pictures of vector addition. First, place the tail of $\mathbf B$ at the head of $\mathbf A$; the arrow from the tail of $\mathbf A$ to the head of $\mathbf B$ is $\mathbf A+\mathbf B$. Second, place both tails together and complete a parallelogram; its diagonal is the sum. This form makes commutativity visible: $\mathbf A+\mathbf B=\mathbf B+\mathbf A.$ Third, add corresponding components: $C_i=A_i+B_i,
  \qquad i=x,y,z,$ where $\mathbf C=\mathbf A+\mathbf B$. These rules also define arbitrary linear combinations such as $a\mathbf A+b\mathbf B$.

p.src: The dot product

u.src: The dot product
en: The dot product

p.src:
Project $\mathbf A$ on the axis defined by $\mathbf B$. If the angle between the vectors is $\theta$, the signed component of $\mathbf A$ along $\mathbf B$ is $\lvert\mathbf A\rvert\cos\theta$. Multiplying this projection by $\lvert\mathbf B\rvert$ defines $\mathbf A\cdot\mathbf B
  =\lvert\mathbf A\rvert\,\lvert\mathbf B\rvert\cos\theta.$ The result is a scalar, not another vector. Equation  is symmetric in $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$, so $\mathbf A\cdot\mathbf B=\mathbf B\cdot\mathbf A$.

p.src:
The law of cosines follows from the same algebra. Let $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ run from a common vertex to the other two vertices of a triangle. The third side is $\mathbf C=\mathbf A-\mathbf B$, not $\mathbf A+\mathbf B$. Therefore $\begin{aligned}
  C^2
  &=(\mathbf A-\mathbf B)\cdot(\mathbf A-\mathbf B)\notag\\
  &=A^2+B^2-2\mathbf A\cdot\mathbf B\notag\\
  &=A^2+B^2-2AB\cos\theta.
  \end{aligned}$

p.src: Position, Velocity, and Acceleration

u.src: Position, Velocity, and Acceleration
en: Position, Velocity, and Acceleration

p.src:
Choose an origin and let $\mathbf r$ be the position vector from the origin to a particle. Its components are the Cartesian coordinates: $\mathbf r=(x,y,z),
  \qquad
  \lvert\mathbf r\rvert=\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}.$ Changing the origin changes $\mathbf r$, a question we shall postpone. Once the origin is fixed, motion is described by a time-dependent position, $\mathbf r(t)=\bigl(x(t),y(t),z(t)\bigr).$ The trajectory is therefore encoded by three functions of time.

p.src:
Velocity is the time derivative of position: $\mathbf v(t)=\frac{d\mathbf r}{dt}
  =\dot{\mathbf r}(t),
  \qquad
  v_i=\frac{dx_i}{dt}=\dot x_i.$ A dot always denotes a derivative with respect to time. The magnitude $\lvert\mathbf v\rvert$ is the speed. Position and velocity are independent directions in general: a particle at one location may be moving in any direction allowed by the problem.

p.src: Uniform Circular Motion

u.src: Uniform Circular Motion
en: Uniform Circular Motion

p.src: For the final example, let a particle move in the $x$-$y$ plane on the unit circle. It begins on the positive $x$-axis at $t=0$, and its angular coordinate increases uniformly: $\theta(t)=\omega t.$ The constant $\omega$ is the angular frequency. One revolution corresponds to an increase $2\pi$ in the angle, so the period is $T=\frac{2\pi}{\omega}.$ The angle may be allowed to increase beyond $2\pi$; the position repeats even though the continuously recorded angle does not reset.

One revolution corresponds to an increase $2\pi$ in the angle, so the period is $T=\frac{2\pi}{\omega}.$ The angle may be allowed to increase beyond $2\pi$; the position repeats even though the continuously recorded angle does not reset.

One revolution corresponds to an increase $2\pi$ in the angle, so the period is $T=\frac{2\pi}{\omega}.$ The angle may be allowed to increase beyond $2\pi$; the position repeats even though the continuously recorded angle does not reset.

p.src:
On the unit circle, $\mathbf r(t)
  =\bigl(\cos\omega t,\,\sin\omega t\bigr).$ Differentiation gives $\mathbf v(t)
  =\omega\bigl(-\sin\omega t,\,\cos\omega t\bigr).$ The velocity is tangent to the circle. We can prove its perpendicularity to the radius without relying on the drawing: $\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf r\cdot\mathbf v
  &=\cos\omega t\,(-\omega\sin\omega t)
    +\sin\omega t\,(\omega\cos\omega t)\notag\\
  &=0.
  \end{aligned}$

  &=0.
  \end{aligned}$

p.src:
Because the radius is one, $\lvert\mathbf r\rvert=1,
  \qquad
  \lvert\mathbf v\rvert=\omega,
  \qquad
  \lvert\mathbf a\rvert=\omega^2.$ Increasing $\omega$ increases the speed linearly and the required inward acceleration quadratically. For a circle of radius $R$, the same calculation would give $v=\omega R$ and $\lvert\mathbf a\rvert=\omega^2R=v^2/R$; the lecture uses $R=1$ to keep the first calculation uncluttered.

p.src: We now have the elementary language needed for particle mechanics: states and initial data, reversible evolution, coordinates, vectors, and the derivatives that define velocity and acceleration. The next task is to decide exactly which initial data specify a particle and to find laws that carry those data from one instant to the next.
